title: Reverse Words in a String II
statement:
`s` is an array of single characters that spells out a sentence: words made of English letters and digits, every two neighbouring words separated by exactly one space `' '`, and no space at the start or the end. Reverse the order of the words, so the last word comes first and the first word comes last, while the characters inside each word keep their order and the single spaces stay between words.

Change `s` itself and return nothing. Do it in place, with only O(1) extra memory: no second array, string or list of words.
constraints: s[i] is an English letter (upper or lower case), a digit, or a space ' '
s contains at least one word
s has no leading or trailing spaces
Words in s are separated by exactly one space
notes:
## Intuition

Reversing the whole array puts the words in the right order, but spells each one backwards. Reversing every word a second time fixes the spelling without moving the word. Both steps are plain two-pointer reversals that swap characters inside `s`, so no extra array is needed. Splitting into a list of words and joining them back is simpler, but it allocates memory the problem forbids.

## Approach

1. `reverse(left, right)` swaps `s[left]` and `s[right]` and moves both pointers toward the middle until they meet.
2. Reverse the whole array: `reverse(0, s.length - 1)`.
3. Scan with `end` from 0 to `s.length`, with `start` marking where the current word begins.
4. When `end` reaches a space or the end of the array, the word is `s[start..end-1]`: reverse it, then set `start = end + 1`, the first character after the space.

## Example 1, step by step

`s` spells `the sky is blue`. Reversing everything gives `eulb si yks eht`. The scan then finds `eulb` (indices 0–3) and turns it into `blue`, then `si` into `is`, `yks` into `sky` and, at the end of the array, `eht` into `the`. The array now spells `blue is sky the`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n): each character is swapped at most twice and scanned once.
- Space: O(1): only a few indices and one temporary character.

## Pitfalls

- Let `end` run up to `s.length` inclusive, or the last word is never reversed back.
- The word before a space ends at `end - 1`, and the next one starts at `end + 1`; off-by-one errors here leave a space inside a word.
- `s.join('').split(' ')` is quick to write but breaks the O(1) extra space rule.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `left`, `right` | the two ends of the stretch being reversed |
| `temp` | holds one character during a swap |
| `start` | index of the first character of the current word |
| `end` | scanning index; a space or `s.length` marks the end of a word |
